Quando penso a un regista, con uno stile arrogante e privo di sostanza, mi viene sempre in mente Ryūsuke Hamaguchi. Drive My Car più che un film pare una presa per il culo di 3 ore, con scene al limite del cringe, lunguaggini inutili e soluzioni narrative scontate e involontariamente divertenti. È un film banalmente noioso, ripetitivo, e con una messa in scena piatta e televisiva. Sostenuto da attori che recitano come dei manichini e da una scrittura degna di un surreale libro di Federico Moccia. Chiunque consideri Hamaguchi un maestro del cinema moderno si è fatto abbindolare da un grande paraculo.

Such a pathetic old man bro 😭 This movie really did not need to be almost 3 hours long because this really wasn’t it for me. “Ohhh but he’s supposed to be like that because the movie is about how he deals with his grief.” Yeah, I fucking know that, bro. And because he’s supposed to be like that, I’m also allowed to fucking hate his sorry ass. His character development still made me mad as hell, and the way he handles his grief is giving LOSER ENERGY throughout the entire movie. And holy shit, the scene where he literally sees his wife cheating on him and then just fucking walks away? That was the real embodiment of a loser and a stupid ass man. Bro really stood there, processed the information, and decided, “Yeah, I’m just gonna leave.” I know the whole point is that he’s emotionally repressed and doesn’t know how to confront his feelings, but watching that shit still made me want to punch the screen. But despite how much I fucking hate this type of main character, I have to admit there are so many scenes here that are genuinely beautiful. Especially all those moments when they’re driving around in the car and the camera slowly zooms out, revealing the entire area around them. There’s something so peaceful and almost hypnotic about those shots. The movie can be painfully slow, but visually, I can’t deny that it knows exactly how to create an atmosphere. And the dinner scene with his coworker and his wife who can’t speak? That shit was genuinely moving. It’s one of those scenes where barely anything needs to happen, but the emotion just fucking lands. The way they communicate without being able to communicate normally was probably one of the few moments where I completely understood why people love this movie. My friend actually told me a few years ago that this movie was probably not for me, but I thought, “Nah, I’ve watched enough movies now. I’m ready to step outside my comfort zone.” And to be fair, I’ve actually managed to do that before. I used to hate Linda Linda Linda, and now I fucking love that movie. But this one? Nah man. I can appreciate the aesthetics, the quiet atmosphere, the beautiful cinematography, and some genuinely touching scenes, but spending almost three hours with this fucking loser was still not an experience I enjoyed 😭 I genuinely wanted to laugh in this old man’s face and punch him just because I fucking could. Bro is a loser anyway.

Anton Chekhov’s ‘ Uncle Vanya ’ remains a poignant critique throughout, ever the more preeminent with our delightful cast mirroring the very characters they seek to portray. Chekhov masterfully executes the inevitability of human degeneration— allegorically, a timeless reminder of the physical and moral depletion of mankind. One incredibly forthright in their insistence on stagnating in the cyclical nature of futility. This… less than enduring show of resilience is made ever the more sickening knowing it’s inescapable truth wherein Yamaga’s narrative arc mirrors the play in such juvenile, mimicking irony: nothing changes. (Nothing ever happens). Much like Oto (Cuckmaster General) her husband is more than happy to co-pretend as though there has been no discernible alteration. All is well. Well…apart from the chilling notion that there is no longer any thrill in deviating from the mundanity of domestic life just as there is in participating within it; as Oto self-actualises, the world may have seemed serene, but such placidity was indeed sinister: “ I definitely killed that man ”. Drive My Car shares its name with a short and fun song by The Beatles , but it’s quite the opposite. Not short, nor fun. A long, quiet, slow-burn trauma bond that never fully clicked for me. Like a melodramatic play, ‘twas grade-A crapola. Critically acclaimed, subtitled snoozefest 😴 I’ll admit, I was already burnt out on slow burns, so seeing the 3-hour runtime didn’t help, but I didn’t realize how much that would be felt. I was confused by the opening; relationship dynamics felt unclear, emotional beats didn’t land cleanly, and by the time the “2 years later” card and intro credits hit (40 minutes in!), I was still trying to piece together that overlong prologue I just saw. After that, it settles into a slow moving, very talky, theatre folk drama with lots of subtlety, themes of infidelity, shared grief, and not ever truly knowing someone. It never felt impactful enough to justify the length. I struggled to stay engaged, and 3hrs of subtitles felt like work rather than immersion. Some foreign films completely absorb me to the point I forget I’m reading; this wasn’t one of them. This one made me feel very outside of everything. Not bad, just not for me. Maybe I’m missing some nuance, but from my POV it feels very overrated. Of course a movie about driving a car will have some nice sweeping shots and cinematography, but it wasn’t incredible, nothing I haven’t seen before, and that plot just wasn’t very captivating. It only finally begins to open up a bit in the last stretch, but by then it’s like… that’s it? A long road to a simple idea. This could’ve been a short film.

O filme é muito bem filmado, tem bons diálogos, ótimos visuais e principalmente boas atuações, porém a história não nos cativou o suficiente. As 3 horas do filme passam muito devagar e mesmo entendendo a história, o filme e os personagens não nos prenderam. O filme trata o luto de uma forma complexa e trata da "recuperação" desse luto baseado nas conexões humanas, principalmente demonstradas pela relação do protagonista com sua motorista, na qual inicia muito distante e vai ganhar intimidade a pronto de criar uma conexão. Portanto, apesar do filme ter conquistado milagres de fãs, não nos agradou tanto assim.

Sinceramente, nem sei o que comentar. Na minha visão, é um enredo sem proposito, não há um objetivo claro. No decorrer do filme, os personagens até são desenvolvidos, mas pra quê? Esse filme não tem um sentido para ser assistido.

i did not like this movie. i do not think it is a very good movie. yes, it's well-crafted, yes, i suppose it is conceptually quite rich (i can see many potential essays about the role of voice in the movie, language, acting and known/unknown selves, etc), but when i watch a movie i'm looking to *feel* something, and drive my car left me feeling nothing. there is a real mismatch between the emotional weight of the experiences the characters have and how we see the character act. obv this is not a problem in and of itself. the problem is that the film sustains this mismatch for far too long, and the characters began, at some point, to feel not hurt/traumatized/in shock but simply flat. the ending scene in the snow, which is meant as a moment of catharsis, produced no real impact on me because i was so alienated from these characters. it was like watching robots have breakdowns. the film also failed, imo, to satisfactorily develop kafuku and misaki's relationship. i really think misaki's actress was robbed of screen time. did we really need all those rehearsal scenes? it was also extremely annoying to find the manic pixie dream girl trope rearing its head in BOTH of the main female characters, who seemed to only exist to accessorize kafuku's character. (i am so damn tired of these 'dead wife' movies. solaris. paris, texas. it's misogyny dressed up in a nice color grade.) i absolutely adore evil does not exist, hamaguchi's most recent film, so i came into this expecting to love it. i still think he's a really talented filmmaker, and there are some scenes in here i loved (the hands out the skylight w/ the cigarettes immediately comes to mind), but it just completely missed the emotional chords it was trying to hit.

Almost twenty-four hours since I finished watching this, and I'm still undecided how I feel about it. In theory, it has all the makings of a great film. I look at it and can objectively point out why so many people absolutely love it. But it did not speak to me as much as I'd hoped it would. The premise is mainly centered around grief and how the central characters unravel and deal with its many layers. For a film that is supposed to be so emotional, I found the characters weirdly hollow and empty—not as 'result-of-grief' empty but as 'one-dimensionally-written-character' empty. Oto's characterization is downright awful, but given Murakami's reputation for writing female characters, I wasn't surprised. Apart from that, only a couple of interactions between the characters stand out, and the rest are mostly forgettable. The film's core message is that people are complex, and it is never truly possible to understand another person. And while I get that and agree with it, I think that's not a good enough justification for some people's decisions (looking at you, Oto) that they make at others' expense. Moreover, asking a grieving person to forgive the person who wronged him and whose death he is grieving because "it's just who she was. She was a complex person" is not a kind or rational thing to do and that too from an unreliable person like Takatsuki? No, thanks. I feel like the film does that various times—it shifts blame from the perpetrator to the victim. Kafuku blames himself for not acting a certain way when his wife cheats on him, and Watari believes she's a murderer for not saving her abusive mother. While I understand that grief affects our logic and manifests in unknown ways, Drive My Car, not once, tries to subvert their line of thinking and by the end has almost established that it was, indeed, their fault. Coming to the things I liked—it is beautifuly shot and despite being a three-hour film, I didn't think it was slow or boring. Kafuku and Watari's bond is potrayed beautifuly. Green Book for the arthouse crowd - Armond White Surely no masterpiece - David Stratton Reasonably happy that a 3 hour Japanese film with multiple meta-narratives which asks of some familiarity with Chekhov from the audience has proven so popular. I much preferred a very different film festival darling from 2021, the gritty and strangling Hive from Kosovo which ran a tight 80 minutes, but any increased appreciation for more challenging cinema is respectable. Whilst it would be nice for recent slow cinema diamonds like Long Day's Journey Into Night (2018) or Inside the Yellow Cocoon Shell (2023) to share in some of this success I much prefer to discuss this film over Don't Look Up or Squid Game which seemed to dominate cultural conversation that year. The strength of the film is this running theme that 'we are the love we have lost' and how that manifests in different ways for various personality types. On this, the text succeeds, it is humanist and relatable. There are moving moments, I like the smoking through the sunroof and the closing lines of Uncle Vanya delivered through sign language from a mute Sonya (Park Yu-rim) and particularly enjoyed the scene of Yūsuke (Hidetoshi Nishijima) observing his wife's infidelity then leaving quietly. I also love the Saab, great car choice. Length is not so much the issue, it is the inability for the film to stay focused which lets it down. A generation raised on meandering television series seems not to mind this but I still expect a level of purposeful refinement to writing and craft to pacing. The cinematography is also done in the modern adroit style, cuts to a still shot with an object entering the scene with speed or a slow dissolve between spinning wheels and spinning tape on a cassette. I don't mind when this style is used for intention over design ( Past Lives ) but too often the objective is the aesthetic. What to say about the connections to Chekhov? Burin described it as "both wide-of-the-mark and on-the-nose" which I like, the play material either feels abstract from the emotional malaise or stops still to show direct connection. I like that it took such a difficult shot at it though with the multilingual angle. Vanya on 42nd Street definitely handled the material better but it was a smart move to take a different approach here. Landscapes were beautiful.

Ma bio devient trompeuse à la base je voulais pas faire de critiques Donc par démagogie ce qui est dit n’est pas sérieux C’est assez compliqué de structurer ma pensée, mon rapport même avec le cinéma de Hamaguchi est assez ambivalent. Il est capable de mille grâces et même d’atteindre la perfection, mais de l’autre face de la pièce, ici il y a des point que je n’aime vraiment pas dont la notamment la mise en scène et certain détail de l’histoire. Peut-être qu’il a trop de budget, cette manière de filmer avec plein de plans courts, plein d’angles différents, d’un côté, de l’autre, en bas, d’un angle particulier, etc etc. J’ai pas les termes d’école du cinéma et je m’en fiche des champs, contre-plongées, machin chouette mais ici ça m’agace. On ne peut pas profiter de l’histoire qui est posée. C’est une question de rythme la mise en scène n’est pas en accord avec le récit je trouve après j’avoue il y a quand même pas mal de plan très bien. Il y a trois scènes que je trouve particulièrement magnifiques, mais qui sont gâchées par ces changements de plans. Oui j’assume ma thérapie Hong Sang-soo m’y a conforté je suis un bandeur de plans séquences, de plans fixes et, globalement, de mise en scène légère. J’ai juste envie qu’on me pose dans un coin et que je puisse profiter sans qu’on me déplace tout le temps. Quel gâchis lors du repas, en présence de ma seule raison de suivre le film, j’ai oublié le nom de sont rôle, mais celle qui est muette. Je repense encore au cinéma d’HSS… Il y a aussi la scène de répétition dehors, sous les arbres qui se défeuillent. La scène pourrait être gracieuse, mais la mise en scène la gâche. Et pour finir la troisième scène qui a retenu mon attention c’est celle qui aurait dû être la scène finale à mon humble avis, la dernière scène au théâtre, que je ne décrirai pas qui aller sur se coup ça va et c’était vraiment magnifique Et sur le fond du récit, ce que je n’aime pas, c’est qu’il raconte trop d’histoires dramatiques. Il y a notre protagoniste, mais il y a aussi l’histoire de la chauffeuse, celle qui drive his car la Saab rouge, et celui qui trompe sa femme. Ça alourdi tellement l’histoire. Et puis ce regroupement dans un récit d’histoires atypiques et dramatiques, ça me saoule. Je retrouve ce que je n’aime pas dans Asako 1 & 2 il en fait trop pour tout, pas dans le jeu d’acteur heureusement comparé à dans justement asako ou il en font des caisse ici ça va, mais dans les histoires vécues et dans la mise en scène c’est lourdingue. J’ai quand même profité de la beauté du film, des plans de kiffeur sur la petite voiture qui fait vroum, des plans d’Hiroshima puis dans les montagne enneigées. Le film est beau et a plein de qualités, j’aime bien le prologue et globalement le cœur de l’histoire le deuil et le théâtre. Le film aurait pu me plaire s’il n’était pas aussi lourd. Le sommet de mes reproches, c’est lors du fameux dialogue dans la voiture, vers la fin de la deuxième heure je dirais, entre le type qui trompe sa femme et le protagoniste mari et veuf. Cette ramification avec ce type pour l’incruster dans l’histoire me saoulait. Tout me saoulait avec ce type. Je voulais qu’il soit juste vecteur de deuil et de remords pour le protagoniste, mais il prend une place démesurée dans le récit et puis, accessoirement il me saoule. Et donc le dialogue c’est l’enfer. Et pire, la manière dont il est filmé on filme l’un puis l’autre, et ça alterne champs contrechamps au milieu de l’échange qui me gave au plus haut point. Et j’ai repensé à un autre film qu’il a réalisé que j’ai beaucoup aimé, Contes du hasard et autres fantaisies, où il y a une scène entre deux personnes à l’arrière d’une voiture qui est parfaite, un plan fixe qui filme les deux personnes. C’est pas le même ton dans l’échange, mais c’était beau, là. Je comprend ici la recherche de tension dans les regard dans l’opposition et j’avoue ce qui me déplaît finalement c’est la confrontation avec je sais pas si c’est un plot twist mais du moins la réalisation de certain aspect méconnu je déteste ça en fait c’est l’ensemble la manière dont ces amener la manière dont ces raconter supplée de la mise en scène. Bref, autre point qui fait redondance sur la mise en scène, le théâtre est gâché aussi. Heureusement, il s’est repris et l’a bien fait dans son dernier film, Soudain. Car les plans depuis les tribunes puis tourné vers les spectateurs après devant la scène puis derrière et encore sur le côté et ensuite dans les coulisses et il filme uniquement les moments dramatiques où ça crie, ça gesticule, ça tire au pistolet… Je vois ça et je me dis en plus d’être un piètre metteur en scène pour le cinéma, il l’est aussi pour le théâtre ce qui vu comme ça parais logique. Tout fois je doit dire l’avant dernière scène malgré tout m’a réconcilié. Je retire un peu d’aigreur dans mes propos J’aime bien Hamaguchi. Ça sent qu’il est profondément attentionné dans les sujets sur lesquels il réalise des films mais des fois pour bien faire il ne faut pas en faire trop. Parole sans valeur venant de ma part mais avis honnête.

I like a lot of different parts of this film. But to quickly sum up my feelings, I feel as if “The juice is not worth the squeeze” with this one.. I hate to feel that way as there’s a lot of things to like about this film, it’s just the time it takes to get there. The film has a general slow pace which I don’t mind in films, it’s the execution. There’s a lot of scene developing subtext about characters and their emotions towards one another, not a lot of dialogue and usually if it is it’s not directly saying what is true to the moment. WHICH is the point of the film, but I just never found the dialogue itself and the issues at hand to always be interesting enough to warrant this technique or development to be so prominent throughout the runtime. Then there’s portions where you are getting somewhere and….it’s….getting…there….just….keeeep……waiting……we’re…..THERE. I actually loved those moments for what it’s worth, it’s just that the pacing is already slow as molasses and the better moments in themselves is slow as well. The opening credits rolled around the 45 min mark and that just mentally did something to me, when I realized how that opening portion of the film was meant to actually start the movie. Something that I feel could have been shortened from 45 minutes to about 15-20 with effective dialogue and pacing. It’s hard to really harp on a director on pacing when most of that is intentional in this case. You can feel it’s meant to be a slow grind to the finish line for the pay off to feel that much more emotionally rewarding to see, yet I felt like the finishing beats of the film are something you can read on the characters face the entire time and a lot of the “filler” I experienced was for something I expected the whole time. There’s a few good moments throughout this run time like I said earlier, I enjoy parts. I love most scenes with the driver, this is a character that I think has good interactions with the lead to really break Yūsukes walls down. Her story really came full circle at the end which felt good, yet sometimes in certain emotional moments there’s a point where the dialogue really gets on the nose with things like “AND THIS EMOTIONAL MOMENT IN MY LIFE CAN SERVE AS A LESSON TO YOU BTW….” For a film that’s subtle throughout its entire run, it sort of blows its figurative load randomly throughout the film and seems to have a hard time finding a balance between nuance and convenient dialogue. Something I did like about the film is some of the themes in particular the overhead theme of grief and how you can grieve someone you have complicated feelings about. How hard it may be to let go of certain ideas about this person, that there isn’t going to be a reconciliation. The complexities of human relationships, how one person can never truly be understood 100% even through years and years of a relationship. There are always different sides of us as we grow and change. It’s about adapting, growing, challenging yourself and coming to grips with hard truths. The car scene between Yūsuke & Takatsuki is probably the best directed bit and best written portion of the film. It’s a payoff inside about the last hour of the film. The performances across the board are good, especially the lead, if not a little drab seeing him almost never smile and just look melancholic almost the whole film. Overall I think this just felt like overly long for myself and that could it be cutdown at least half an hour at minimum and have its emotional effectiveness still hit.

Drive My Car no es una película sobre aprender a vivir con una pérdida. Es, quizá, una película sobre descubrir que nunca terminamos de conocer a las personas que amamos. Kafuku pasa buena parte de su vida intentando descifrar a Oto: sus silencios, sus infidelidades, las historias que inventa, aquello que calla. Pero cuando ella muere, descubre una paradoja devastadora: a veces la muerte no nos arrebata solamente a una persona, sino también la posibilidad de hacerle las preguntas que dejamos para después. Quizá amar sea convivir con esa clase de incertidumbre. La película parece decir que escuchar no siempre significa alcanzar al otro. Podemos conocer su voz, sus gestos, sus rutinas y hasta sus heridas, y aun así existir frente a una habitación interior cuya puerta nunca se abre del todo. Por eso el auto funciona como algo más que un escenario: es un espacio de confesión. Dos desconocidos avanzan durante horas sin mirarse directamente, y paradójicamente, en esa ausencia de mirada consiguen verse de verdad. Misaki y Kafuku no se salvan mutuamente; simplemente se reconocen en el lugar donde ambos están rotos. Y quizá ahí está lo más hermoso: no necesitamos resolver el dolor de alguien para acompañarlo. La película también cuestiona esa idea romántica de que amar significa conocer al otro por completo. Tal vez sea exactamente al contrario. Amar es aceptar que el otro siempre conservará una parte de sí mismo que no nos pertenece. Hay algo profundamente humano en nuestra necesidad de encontrar explicaciones: creemos que ponerle palabras a una herida hará que duela menos. Pero algunas heridas no se cierran cuando encontramos una respuesta, sino cuando dejamos de exigirla. Drive My Car me dejó pensando que el duelo no consiste solamente en extrañar a alguien, sino en aprender a vivir con todo lo que nunca sabremos de esa persona. Y quizás amar a alguien sea también hacer las paces con ese misterio. ¿Es posible conocer verdaderamente a alguien a quien amamos, o el amor exige abrazar la imposibilidad de comprenderlo por completo?

Haruki Murakami adaptations, from what I've triangulated between this and Burning, aren't really my thing. The work seems to attract a generally high-quality, but tedious, brand of festival-circuit sycophancy, and people speak about these films in hushed, reverent tones. I'm genuinely unsure why. Drive My Car is a slow, tender, thoughtful, beautiful film that bored me to tears with its literary fluffiness. The entire three-hour runtime—way, way too long—is starved of any proairetic momentum except driving around. Most of this film is either watching people put on a play, or watching people drive around Japan having polite conversations about their feelings. This movie sleepwalks. I watch films late at night like a ghoul, because I'm a ghoulish guy, and somnambulist pacing like this makes me want to check my phone, not escape into daydreams. I'm sure many people love this vibe, but this one missed me. This didn't move me at all. Kafuku—a screamingly obvious nod to Kafka—is an insufferable protagonist. His central conceit is writing plays while banging somebody, a process that strikes me as intensely selfish and stupid and abstract. He casts his multilingual play with actors who do not speak the same language, let alone Japanese, forcing scripts translated from Russian into Japanese. Throw in a randomly deaf woman speaking Korean sign language while her husband translates, and the whole affair reveals itself as arbitrarily and performatively intersectional. It's so late 2010s, and early 2020s that my eyes are rolling. It adds meaningless abstraction disguised as intellectual rigor. The overarching thesis is that Murakami thinks that we must come to terms with the fact that you can never truly know someone. That's tautologically true, but practically a bit. My wife and I know each other better than we know ourselves. Intimacy is entirely possible; it just belongs to a different story, one where people talk directly to each other instead of hiding behind artistic metaphors like insufferable intellectuals, art majors, or theater kids. Nobody in this film manages a fundamental human connection despite several sex scenes and many profound personal conversations, which Murakami assumes is universal but feels fundamentally paradoxical from someone so perspicacious. This doesn't seem like a reflection of the world as much as a reflection of how Murakami views it, and nothing about it resonates with my personal experience. The film bootstraps its own credibility by stealing wholesale from Uncle Vanya and Waiting for Godot, putting on fake theatrical productions of whole scenes from these plays. But if you're going to mask a narratively anemic script behind other people's dramatic work, please don't choose plays I've been in, and totally fucking hated. Visually, there's some shots in this that sparkle. The cigarettes out the sunroof is awesome. The image of the car's wheels turning into spinning cassette tapes is a visual pun I'm amazed I've never seen before. But the physical logic of the titular car drives me insane. Kafuku insists on riding in the backseat of a left-hand-drive Saab turbo coupe. First of all, a pristine, left-hand-drive Saab in Japan is an absurd novelty; as someone who grew up in Vermont, I've seen a million Saab 900 Turbos, and this is the shiniest one I or anyone else has ever seen. That shininess is LIES. I demand my Swedish cars be like my Swedish licorice-salted into oblivion. Second, the back seats of those coupes suck, even if you're a smaller framed guy. I haven't been in one since the 90's but it's hard to get back there in the first place. You would naturally sit up front in your own damn car, and you'd wear your seatbelt. The director forces this no-seatbelt, back-seat staging purely to represent interpersonal distance, completely ignoring how fundamentally stupid and unrealistic it is. Maybe this is explained away in the book, but I ain't reading it to find out. And maybe this film, with its distant, technical competence resonates with people who have endured profound loss or a devastating breakup. But not me. I like to think I could fix this film by cutting out the first forty minutes and shortening all those stage-play sequences. The opening credits don't even hit until those first forty minutes are up, because the first 40 minutes are a prologue whose absence would better serve the thesis of the film. However, that would remove all the cool parts of the movie, and by that I mean all the nudity. The movie opens directly to an artful shot of boobs and a butt, and we can't lose that--not when the rest of the film will be so boring in comparison. The boobs must stay, so Uncle Vanya has GOT to go. Hansi's June Film Class

A film about grief, intimacy, guilt, and how little we can ever truly know another person. Loved how the red saab becomes this private space between solitude and connection, where Yusuke and Misaki slowly recognize the same guilt in each other without ever needing to completely explain themselves. Uncle vanya slowly becomes more than a play within the film. The multilingual rehearsals, repetition, sign language… all blur the line between performing and actually confronting yourself. Acting becomes another language for feelings you can’t say as yourself. Such an impressive way to weave a play through three hours where even the lines we understand seem to quietly serve the film’s message. So subtle. Grief lingers through the slow pacing and endless drives, which somehow gave me a bittersweet sense of peace. And that Hokkaido journey with the red car surrounded by snow finally gives them the space to say what they’ve been carrying. Not forgiveness, not closure, just acceptance. Then misaki inherits the saab. The same car that carried Yusuke through his grief, memories, and loneliness now carries her. Maybe that’s all there is to it sometimes. You carry what you’ve lost, you get behind the wheel and you keep the car moving.

Un périple rempli à la fois de mélancolie et de chaleur humaine, une véritable balade à l'atmosphère oscillant entre la profonde tristesse provenant de passés douloureux, et un sentiment d'apaisement. À l'intérieur de cette voiture rouge difficile à rater, nous allons assister à la rencontre de deux êtres blessés et égarés. Dans cette sorte de cocon permettant au protagoniste d'échapper au dehors, cette espèce de symbole de son intimité, de son monde intérieur où il s'est renfermé sur lui-même, une chauffeuse viendra s'y introduire, cette deuxième âme esquintée qui deviendra progressivement pour le personnage principal une compagnie précieuse, une semblable avec laquelle il développera une relation de confiance, transformant petit à petit ce qui était un environnement de solitude et d'isolement en un refuge, un lieu de partage et de guérison pour deux individus aux plaies encore ouvertes, une voiture avec laquelle ils partiront vers un voyage introspectif. Avec Drive My Car, Ryusuke Hamaguchi démontre une nouvelle fois sa capacité à fluidifier et teinter d'authenticité ses métrages. Le film se déroule lentement, soigneusement, en laissant tout le temps à son spectateur de s'imprégner de son ambiance naturelle. Je me suis vraiment complètement senti absorbé par ces silences, ces instants de calme presque aérien, cette mise en scène utilisant les espaces, les environnements, les regards ou encore de simples gestes pour illustrer l'intériorité des personnages avec subtilité, mais aussi toutes ces discussions parfois chaleureuses, et à d'autres moments beaucoup plus lourdes, quand les fêlures étouffées refont finalement surface. Il y a une profonde humanité qui se dégage de ce film, notamment lorsque Hamaguchi va, autour d'une pièce de théâtre servant de fil conducteur, présenter des personnages d'horizons distincts, certains avec des origines différentes, s'exprimant avec d'autres langues, et même un autre ayant un handicap avec lequel il parvient à vivre. On sent que le réalisateur tient à dépeindre tout ce qui fait la richesse de l'humain, que ce soit en montrant les différences apparentes, mais aussi en explorant des vécus qui n'ont rien à voir entre eux. À travers cette pièce de théâtre et les récits gravitant autour, ayant comme le dit si bien le film le pouvoir de faire ressortir toute la subtilité et la profondeur des sentiments, ainsi que les interactions entre nos deux protagonistes qui sont parfois remplies d'échanges et parfois simplement silencieuses, Hamaguchi explore les différents chemins pour espérer franchir la terrible épreuve qu'est le deuil et tenter de soulager son mal-être, un moyen d'avancer malgré ce trou béant provoqué par la perte et la culpabilité, qui se trouverait donc dans le partage, l'introspection et l'extériorisation. Faire preuve d'honnêteté et faire la paix avec soi-même, accepter ses erreurs, ses regrets, ce qui ne peut être changé, et rester malgré tout ouvert au reste du monde, c'est pour moi ce que prône Drive My Car, cette sublime parenthèse de vie pleine d'humanité qui m'aura complètement transporté.

The first time I saw this was on release, and it remains one of my favorite moviegoing experiences. I caught a late showing in my college town, walked out around 1am, and still had time to grab a burger and a drink at one of my favorite bars. I gave it five stars then — it left me with a strange, specific peace I couldn't fully explain. About four years later, I hit play again and realized how much I'd actually forgotten. It felt almost like a first viewing, except this time I was older, a little wiser, and genuinely stunned by how good the script is. It would be easy to assume the film is simply "inspired" by Murakami's short story of the same name, but it's actually weaving together at least two more stories from the same collection — "Kino" and "Scheherazade" — alongside Chekhov's Uncle Vanya, which functions as the film's central framing device, mirroring the protagonist's emotional state and his relationship to his own grief. None of it feels clunky or bolted on — it's fully absorbed into the film's own language. What struck me most this time is how the despair on screen never too feel harsh toward the viewer — but the tension is there. It's life, distilled: that inevitable state of living and missing, of loss that doesn't resolve so much as scar over. And still — you move forward. Maybe that's the most human thing there is.

Not all three-hour movies are going to be GOATs. For every GODFATHER/GODFATHER PART II, you are going to get a MEET JOE BLACK. Happily, DRIVE MY CAR falls into the former category. The 35-minute prologue set in Tokyo is one of the greatest pieces of cinema I've ever seen. The complex relationship between Hidetoshi Nishijima's protagonist, and Reika Kirishima as his wife -- who features in three sensitive and nuanced explicit love scenes, something you don't find with 48-year-old actresses in Hollywood -- is well-written and well-directed, with a turntable playing Beethoven and a full-length hallway mirror, given Chekhovian introductions. Speaking of Chekhov, the remainder of the film involves NIshijima directing a multilingual performance of "Uncle Vanya" in Hiroshima, with young Toko MIura as a driver he didn't ask for. Six languages are utilized. The cast and theater staff (including Miura) are broken characters who use the play as therapy to explore or heal their wounds, but not every character finds their muse in Chekhov or achieves their happy ending. The three hours fly by. Long silences in a film can be deadly but here the silences invite you to think and reflect. A gorgeous work of art, and the fact that it was made during COVID, with an epilogue set at the height of the pandemic, only makes it more urgent and more interesting.

"It didn't sound like he was lying. I don't know if it's the truth, but he was telling you what was true to him." I don’t really know how to write about Drive My Car. I’ve tried. Every time I think I understand why this movie means so much to me, I realize I’ve only found another part of the answer. It’s one of those movies that I don’t just remember watching. I remember how it felt to watch it. I remember the silence after it ended. I remember sitting there thinking, “How the hell did a movie understand something I couldn’t even put into words?” Maybe that sounds dramatic. I don’t care. Drive My Car means that much to me. What gets me is that this movie understands grief in a way that feels almost unfairly honest. It doesn’t make grief beautiful. It doesn’t turn it into some meaningful journey where you eventually figure everything out and become a better person. Sometimes grief is just there. You wake up with it. You go to work with it. You talk to people while carrying it around. You laugh while carrying it. You fall asleep with it. And sometimes you can go months feeling like you’re fine, only for one tiny thing, a voice, a place, a memory to remind you that you’re not. That’s Yūsuke. He’s surrounded by people, surrounded by art, surrounded by words, and somehow he still can’t say the thing he actually needs to say. I think that’s what hurt me the most. Because how many times do we do that? How many things do we leave unsaid because saying them would make them real? How many conversations do we replay in our heads because we never got the chance to have them properly? How many people do we lose without ever really knowing them? The movie doesn’t give Yūsuke the closure he wants. And I think that’s why I love it. Because sometimes you don’t get closure. Sometimes the person you needed an explanation from is no longer there to give it to you. Sometimes you find out something about someone you loved that changes the way you remember them. Sometimes you realise that you knew someone deeply and didn’t know them at all. And you still have to wake up the next morning. The car is where all of this becomes real for me. There is something about Yūsuke and Misaki sitting in that red Saab that I can’t explain without making it sound smaller than it is. They’re just sitting there. Driving. Talking sometimes. Not talking other times. And somehow those scenes feel more intimate than most romances I’ve ever seen. Because intimacy isn’t always touching someone. Sometimes it’s being quiet beside someone and not feeling like you have to fill the silence. Sometimes it’s letting someone see the parts of you that you normally keep buried. Sometimes it’s just trusting someone enough to sit beside you while you’re hurting. I love that Yūsuke and Misaki don’t magically fix each other. They don’t. They just recognize something in each other. Two people carrying things they don’t know how to put down. And maybe that’s enough. The Uncle Vanya scenes destroyed me too. Especially because Yūsuke knows these words so well, but knowing the words doesn’t mean he’s ready to hear them. That’s basically the entire movie. We spend so much of our lives talking. Explaining. Defending ourselves. Trying to make other people understand us. But Drive My Car made me think about how rarely we actually listen. Really listen. And maybe that’s why Misaki becomes so important to Yūsuke. She listens without trying to solve him. She doesn’t demand that he explain everything. She just stays. That kind of presence feels incredibly rare. And then there’s Oto. I love that the movie doesn’t make her into some perfect dead wife whose only purpose is to make us feel sorry for Yūsuke. She’s complicated. She loved him. She hurt him. He loved her. He didn’t understand her. There were things happening inside her that he never got to fully know. And now he’s left with all of these contradictions. I think that’s one of the most painful things about losing someone: you don’t just lose the person. You lose the possibility of ever learning anything else about them. There are questions that become permanently unanswered. And you have to learn how to live with that. I don’t think Drive My Car taught me how to move on. I think it taught me that maybe “moving on” isn’t even the right way to think about it. You don’t necessarily leave things behind. You carry them differently. You carry people. You carry memories. You carry mistakes. You carry things you wish you’d done differently. And eventually, somehow, you learn how to keep going with all of it inside you. That’s what the title means to me now. Drive. Keep going. Not because everything is okay. Not because you’ve forgotten. Not because you’ve forgiven everyone or figured yourself out. Just because the road is still there. And maybe someone is sitting beside you. Maybe you don’t even have to talk. Maybe, for a little while, you just need someone else in the car. I don’t know if I’ve ever loved a movie this quietly. It doesn’t scream at me. It doesn’t tell me what to feel. It just sits there. And somehow, every time I come back to it, it finds a different part of me. I think that’s why I keep coming back. Because Drive My Car doesn’t feel like a movie I watched. It feels like a place I’ve been. And I don’t think I’ll ever really leave it.

Asks the essential human question on how do we continue to choose to live in spite of everything. Drive My Car is a film of reserved stillness that rewards the patient, really fell into this one. Ambient, slow and steady yet full of humanistic integrity, Hamaguchi’s rendition lifts Murakami's 20 or so page short story about an isolated man dialoging through his past and turns it into an incredibly ambitious project concerning art, personhood, grief, transference through creation, and acceptance. The creative liberties it takes with the initial story turns it from a compelling piece about two people conversing into an incisive and engaging treatise on the anatomy of melancholy and complex yet essential human truths. The words we leave unsaid end up corroding us from the inside out; sometimes all we need is someone not to fix anything for us, but simply to hear us out. Life changes when we move away from drifting inaction and decide to choose every second. To be heard is to feel connected, to be connected is to feel alive, and to feel alive is to save ourselves. Visually gorgeous and the soundtrack had me floating… sometimes films come to you at the right time when you need them, and this one did just that. Can feel myself returning to this one a lot in years to come.
